nameStory: The Featherlegged Orbweaver gets its common name from the distinctive feathery tufts of hair on its legs that look like tiny plumes. These fuzzy leg decorations aren't just for show - they help the spider manipulate its special woolly silk as it builds its circular web.
description: The Featherlegged Orbweaver is a small, delicate spider that builds classic round webs like other orbweavers. What makes this spider truly unique is that it's completely harmless - it has no venom glands at all, making it one of the few non-venomous spiders in North America. Instead of poison, it relies on a special fuzzy, woolly silk called cribellate silk that tangles up prey like cotton batting. These spiders are typically small and brownish, with those characteristic feathery leg hairs that give them their name.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds a classic circular orbweb, but the silk has a distinctly woolly, fuzzy texture that feels almost cottony when you accidentally walk through it - completely different from the sticky, stretchy webs of other orbweavers

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small, elongated body that appears more delicate and slender than most other orbweavers, with a brownish coloration that can vary from light tan to darker brown

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the characteristic feathery tufts of hair on the legs that look like tiny bottle brushes - these are clearly visible and unique among New England spiders

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, may jump from the web, shake it vigorously, or move to the edge - behavior varies depending on time of day and whether egg sacs are present in the web

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Generally smaller and more delicate-looking than common orbweavers, with a body that feels almost weightless if you need to gently relocate one

habitat: Found throughout New England in gardens, woodlands, and shrubby areas where they can anchor their webs between branches or plant stems. They prefer spots with some protection from wind and rain, often building webs in the understory of mixed forests or among garden plants. Look for them in areas with moderate vegetation density where flying insects are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to build their distinctive fuzzy webs in protected spots among emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most visible and spiders are actively hunting. This is the best time to observe their unique woolly silk and feathery legs.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs may be visible in webs. Females show distinctive protective behaviors when egg sacs are present, vigorously shaking the web when disturbed.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off with the first hard frosts, while eggs overwinter in protected silk sacs to emerge the following spring.

funFact: This is one of the only spiders in North America that's completely harmless to everything - it has no venom glands at all and instead catches prey using silk so woolly and tangled that insects get hopelessly stuck like flies in cotton batting!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small orbweavers in the Araneidae family, but the Featherlegged Orbweaver's web silk has a distinctive woolly, non-sticky texture that's completely different from the stretchy, sticky webs of true orbweavers. Memory trick: if the web feels fuzzy rather than sticky on your skin, you've found a featherleg!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'orbweaver,' this spider belongs to a completely different family (Uloboridae) than the true orbweavers (Araneidae). The name similarity comes from their shared web-building style, but they're about as distantly related as two web-building spiders can be.
compareHints: This is the only Uloborus species found in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other members of the hackled orbweaver family (Uloboridae), it's distinguished by its northern range and smaller size. All family members share the trait of being non-venomous and using woolly cribellate silk, but most other species are found in warmer climates further south and west.
